strengths: The paper is well written and provides an unusually thorough and structured review of existing VQ gradient-flow solutions (STE, EMA, RT, ST-GS, NSVQ), with a clear motivation table (Table 1) of desiderata.

The core idea of DiVeQ (directional reparameterization of the quantization error so that the surrogate points at the nearest codeword) is simple, sensible, and a natural improvement over NSVQ's isotropic noise; Fig. 2/3 make the geometric intuition easy to follow.
SF-DiVeQ is an interesting attempt to address codebook collapse and codebook–latent misalignment without replacement heuristics, quantizing along a space-filling curve.

The empirical study is extensive: VQ-VAE compression and VQGAN generation across five datasets, multiple bitrates, three random seeds, ablations on batch size, learning rate, and variance sigma^2, plus an RVQ extension and additional qualitative results.
Proposed methods act as drop-in replacements without auxiliary losses, which is practically attractive, and the improved codebook replacement scheme (Sec. B.1) is a useful secondary contribution.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: DiVeQ is essentially NSVQ with a mean-shifted directional noise (v + d instead of v), a small delta from the same research group's prior work (Vali & Bäckström 2022), and SF-DiVeQ directly reuses the authors' SFVQ dithering idea. The reparameterization-trick framing does not add substantial technical depth.

Claims are stronger than the evidence. Table 1 checks 'no hyperparameter tuning' and 'no train–test mismatch' for DiVeQ, yet sigma^2 is a tuned hyperparameter (1e-3 for compression, 1e-2 for generation) and training uses stochastic quantization while inference uses hard VQ — the same train–test mismatch the paper criticizes in NSVQ, merely reduced.

VQGAN generation results are mixed, not uniformly better: in Table 2 and Table 6, STE/EMA/RT frequently beat DiVeQ/SF-DiVeQ at bitrates 10 and 12 (e.g., STE 5.28 vs DiVeQ 6.32 on CELEBA-HQ bitrate 10; RT 4.73 vs DiVeQ 8.22 on FFHQ bitrate 12). The paper reframes this as 'robustify low bitrates,' but the abstract's claim of improving 'sample quality over alternative quantization approaches' overstates the results. Compression gains over STE/EMA/ST-GS are also modest.

SF-DiVeQ has significant underspecified aspects: the notion of 'subsequent/consecutive codewords' c_j and c_{j+1} presupposes an ordering of a learned codebook that is never defined; it requires a bespoke training procedure (skip quantization for initial epochs, mean-of-latents initialization), which contradicts the 'no special heuristics' positioning, and it is only applied to one-stage VQ without discussion of how ordering generalizes (e.g., to RVQ or large codebooks).

No rigorous analysis: the gradient computation (Eq. 10) is stated without derivation of bias/variance properties or convergence guarantees; claims of 'unbiased codebook gradients' and avoidance of codebook collapse are asserted rather than analyzed; the misalignment analysis relies on t-SNE visualizations and an informal redefinition of misalignment in terms of rate-distortion violations.
Missing comparison with competitive modern quantization baselines (LFQ, FSQ, BSQ, SimVQ-style methods) that are cited but not benchmarked, which weakens the SOTA claim.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many tuned details (replacement schedules, initialization procedures, per-task sigma^2).

Some technical claims are questionable, e.g., the θ2 = 240° probability argument for NSVQ's error inflation, and there appear to be typographical/data errors in tables (e.g., '619' FID for EMA in Table 6).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper covers two tasks (VQ-VAE compression, VQGAN generation), five datasets, eight bitrates, three random seeds, plus ablations on batch size, learning rate, and variance, and an extension to Residual VQ.

The identification of the directional flaw in NSVQ (Fig. 2: the noise substitution overshoots the true quantization error with ~67% probability) is a clean and correct observation, and DiVeQ's fix (biasing the noise toward the nearest codeword) is simple and sensible.

The analysis of codebook–latent misalignment (Figs. 4, 22, Sec. C.6) and the proposed importance-sampling codebook replacement (Sec. B.1) add useful practical insight for practitioners training VQ models.
The paper is clearly written, with a helpful summary of prior methods (Table 1) and thorough appendices with implementation details.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work. DiVeQ is essentially NSVQ with the noise mean shifted from zero to (ci* - z); the conceptual delta from Vali & Bäckström (2022) is small. SF-DiVeQ likewise combines the authors' own SFVQ (2023) with the same directional-noise idea. The core contribution reads as an incremental refinement rather than a new technique.

The 'no hyperparameter tuning' claim (Table 1, abstract, conclusion) is contradicted by the paper's own results: σ² materially affects performance (σ²=10⁻¹ fails badly; Sec. C.5 concludes σ²=10⁻³ is 'best'), and SF-DiVeQ additionally requires a special training schedule (skipping quantization for initial epochs, mean-of-latents initialization, Sec. A.5). These are effectively hyperparameters and heuristics.

The train–test mismatch criticism leveled against ST-GS and NSVQ applies equally to DiVeQ/SF-DiVeQ: training uses stochastic directional noise while inference uses hard argmin VQ. The paper does not reconcile this inconsistency in its positioning.

Generation results do not support the headline claim of consistent improvement. In Tables 2 and 6, DiVeQ and SF-DiVeQ frequently lose to plain STE and EMA at bitrates 10 and 12 (e.g., FFHQ bitrate 12: RT 4.73 vs DiVeQ 8.22; LSUN Bedroom bitrate 9: STE 4.89 vs DiVeQ 4.87 with SF-DiVeQ 6.01). Gains are largely confined to low bitrates and compression metrics; the text's framing overstates the evidence.

No comparison against the structured-codebook methods the paper itself discusses (FSQ, LFQ, BSQ, RPQ), which are currently the strongest practical alternatives and avoid the gradient problem by design. Their omission weakens the significance of the reported wins over STE/EMA/RT/ST-GS/NSVQ.

The misalignment analysis is largely anecdotal. Defining misalignment as 'the case in which the rate-distortion theory does not hold' (Sec. 4) is circular, and the causal link between misalignment and metric non-monotonicity is only hypothesized, not established (the paper itself uses 'we hypothesize').

Several internal inconsistencies: Table 1 marks DiVeQ as avoiding codebook collapse, yet codebook replacement is applied to DiVeQ in all experiments; Table 1's claim that all baselines are 'prone to codebook misalignment' while Fig. 4 shows only 'milder misalignment' for DiVeQ; and no variance/std is reported for the three-run averages, so small reported gaps cannot be assessed for significance.

Scale and applicability of evidence are narrow: models are small, and no experiment demonstrates the method in a modern large-scale tokenizer setting where STE+EMA with modern tricks currently dominates. For a paper claiming a drop-in replacement for 'deep generative models,' the evidence base is modest.

strengths: Clear motivation and a well-structured comparison of existing VQ gradient-flow solutions (Table 1) that crisply identifies the desiderata (no auxiliary losses, no train-test mismatch, hard forward assignments, codebook utilization) and how the proposed methods satisfy them.

The core idea of DiVeQ — directional reparameterization of the quantization error so the surrogate points at the nearest codeword — is a natural and sensible improvement over NSVQ's isotropic noise, and the geometric analysis (Figs. 2-3, limit analysis in Eq. 9) is intuitive.

SF-DiVeQ is the more interesting contribution: quantizing along codeword-connecting line segments simultaneously mitigates quantization error, avoids codebook collapse/replacement heuristics, and (per Fig. 4) empirically prevents codebook-latent misalignment, which is a practically valuable property.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this topic: VQ-VAE compression on 5 datasets across 8 bitrates with 3 seeds, VQGAN generation, ablations on batch size, learning rate, and variance sigma^2, an extension to Residual VQ, a new codebook replacement proposal with perplexity analysis, and detailed training-log diagnostics (Sec. C.8) showing why perplexity/loss curves do not alone indicate good VQ training.

Methods act as drop-in replacements requiring minimal code changes, making the contributions easy to adopt; implementation details and baselines' configurations (including tuning RT and ST-GS fairly) are well documented.
The analysis connecting rate-distortion violations to codebook-latent misalignment (Sec. 4, C.6) is a nice empirical observation that gives the paper depth beyond a method-only contribution.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of DiVeQ relative to prior work: at the operating variance (sigma^2 in [1e-3, 1e-2]) DiVeQ is essentially NSVQ with the noise variance shrunk toward zero, i.e., zq approaches ci* deterministically. The contribution then reduces to 'reduce the noise', which overlaps substantially with NSVQ (random direction, matched magnitude) and with the deterministic rotation-based transforms of the Rotation Trick; the delta over these baselines is incremental.

The experimental evidence for the headline claim of improved generation quality is mixed: in Tables 2 and 6, DiVeQ is frequently not the best method (EMA and STE often achieve the lowest FID, e.g., on LSUN Church and AFHQ), and improvements over STE/EMA at higher bitrates are absent or reversed (e.g., DiVeQ FID 7.69 vs STE 6.69 on CELEBA-HQ bitrate 12). The claim of consistent superiority holds clearly only for low bitrates.

The very poor FID of NSVQ in generation (48-107) is suspicious relative to its published performance; although the authors state the setup is fair, this anomaly makes the strongest baselines in Fig. 5-7 partly uninformative, and no explanation beyond train-test mismatch is offered.

Key modern structured-quantization baselines (FSQ, LFQ, BSQ, RPQ) are discussed in related work but excluded from the experimental comparison, even though they are the strongest current alternatives that sidestep the gradient problem entirely; the comparisons are restricted to STE/EMA/RT/ST-GS/NSVQ.

Fairness concerns in the setup: all methods use the authors' proposed codebook replacement, but SF-DiVeQ alone uses a different initialization procedure (2 warm-up epochs without quantization, data-dependent codebook init from latent statistics), so SF-DiVeQ is not trained under identical conditions; the claimed advantage of avoiding replacement is thus confounded.

SF-DiVeQ's dependence on 'subsequent codewords' c_i* and c_i*+1 is under-specified: how are codebook entries ordered, and what happens when indices are arbitrary or codebooks are replaced/reinitialized? The construction of the space-filling curve and its sensitivity to codeword indexing are not analyzed.

Claims in Table 1 are asserted rather than proven: e.g., 'unbiased codebook gradients' for DiVeQ despite the argmin selection being ignored in the backward pass, and 'no hyperparameter tuning' while sigma^2 is in practice a tunable variance (with the paper itself recommending 1e-3 for compression and 1e-2 for generation).

No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the FID comparisons in Tables 2 and 6, despite the authors acknowledging that sampling randomness causes FID variability; given the small margins between top methods, statistical support is insufficient.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the proposed replacement heuristic and SF-DiVeQ initialization recipe.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem (non-differentiable VQ in end-to-end training) and the proposed DiVeQ is a simple, well-motivated drop-in modification of NSVQ that aligns the simulated quantization-error direction with the nearest codeword, preserving hard assignments while enabling gradient flow.

The evaluation is unusually broad and thorough: VQ-VAE compression across five image datasets, VQGAN generation with FID, DAC-based speech coding with LSD/MFCC/PESQ/STOI, an extension to Residual VQ, and extensive ablations (variance, batch size, learning rate, codebook replacement, initialization).

The analysis of codebook–latent misalignment (connected to rate-distortion behavior and internal covariate shift) is an interesting empirical contribution, and the t-SNE/perplexity analyses are informative.

Implementation details are comprehensive (Sec. A), code and speech samples are promised, and reproducibility is taken seriously (three runs averaged, multiple codebook sizes, fixed hyperparameters across datasets).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: DiVeQ is an incremental modification of the authors' own NSVQ (changing the direction of the injected noise), and SF-DiVeQ combines SFVQ (also by the same authors) with the same directional-noise idea. The paper leans heavily on self-citations (NSVQ, SFVQ, Vali's thesis), and the positioning as a new family of methods is somewhat inflated relative to the actual delta.

The central 'consistent improvement' claim is not fully supported by the paper's own results: in Table 2 (CELEBA-HQ, HP1), DiVeQ is clearly worse than STE/EMA/RT/ST-GS at 9–12 bits (e.g., 7.69 vs. 5.44–6.69 FID at 12 bits), and DiVeQ itself exhibits misalignment cases (e.g., LSUN Church 9-bit and LSUN Bedroom 9-bit under HP2, FID 228/347), contradicting the narrative that the proposed methods are robust.

Missing comparisons to widely adopted modern quantizers (FSQ, LFQ, BSQ, RPQ), which are acknowledged in related work but excluded from experiments on the grounds that they constrain codebook geometry. For a paper claiming state-of-the-art differentiable VQ, at least FSQ or LFQ baselines on the VQGAN task would be expected.

The 'no auxiliary losses / no heuristics' framing is undercut by the method's own requirements: DiVeQ relies on a newly proposed codebook replacement heuristic applied in all experiments, and SF-DiVeQ requires a custom initialization (skipping quantization for two epochs, codebook initialized from recent latents) plus a modified inference-time mapping onto the space-filling curve. Table 1's checkmark summary is thus somewhat self-serving.

Theoretical analysis is thin. The gradient expressions in Eq. (10) involve a stop-gradient unit vector and are potentially ill-behaved as z approaches the selected codeword; the train–test mismatch (stochastic zq in training vs. hard argmin/curve projection at inference) is dismissed rather than formally characterized, and no analysis of convergence or bias of the resulting gradients is given.

Several claims rest on informal reasoning: the NSVQ failure analysis via the 240°/360° argument (Fig. 2) is a heuristic 2D intuition, and the misalignment hypothesis is validated mainly through t-SNE visualizations and post-hoc identification of rate-distortion violations rather than a controlled causal study.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three application areas (VQ-VAE image compression, VQGAN generation, DAC speech coding), five datasets, multiple codebook sizes, and many ablations (variance, batch size, learning rate, codebook replacement, initialization, RVQ) — well above the typical experimental depth for a methods paper.

The methods are simple drop-in replacements for VQ layers without auxiliary losses, which is practically appealing, and the ablations (e.g., C.6, C.7) honestly probe how much supporting machinery (codebook replacement, custom initialization) contributes.
Comprehensive and well-structured related-work review (Sec. 2) and a useful taxonomic summary (Table 1) of the properties of existing VQ training approaches.
The paper is generally clearly written, with implementation details, hyperparameters, and reproducibility information provided in the appendices.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the authors' own prior work: DiVeQ is essentially NSVQ (Vali & Bäckström, 2022) with the isotropic quantization-error noise replaced by noise biased toward the codeword direction — a very small delta — and SF-DiVeQ is a combination of the authors' SFVQ (2023a) with DiVeQ. The paper reads as an incremental refinement of the same group's prior line rather than a new technique.

The gradient analysis in Eq. (10) appears inconsistent: given z_q = z + ||c_{i*}−z|| · sg[v_d/||v_d||], the derivative w.r.t. z should be 1 + u·(z−c_{i*})/||c_{i*}−z||; as σ²→0 (which the paper advocates), u→(c_{i*}−z)/||c_{i*}−z|| and this gradient approaches zero, meaning the encoder would receive vanishing expected gradients exactly in the regime the paper recommends. The formal gradient properties of the method in its recommended operating regime are never established.

The headline claims of 'no auxiliary losses, no hyperparameter tuning, no heuristics' are undercut by the method's own requirements: SF-DiVeQ needs a custom two-epoch pre-training initialization from latent statistics, and with random initialization it requires a 10–50× elevated codebook learning rate to work (Sec. C.7), plus a chosen σ² — contradicting the framing in Table 1 and the conclusion.

Missing comparisons with strong modern alternatives: FSQ, LFQ, BSQ, and RPQ are discussed in related work but never empirically compared, although they are now standard strong baselines in VQ/tokenizer papers. This weakens the claim of superiority over 'alternative quantization approaches.'

Train–test mismatch claim is questionable: Table 1 marks DiVeQ/SF-DiVeQ as having 'no train–test mismatch,' yet training uses a stochastic mapping (noise added, SF-DiVeQ random interpolation points) while inference uses hard nearest-codeword/curve assignment — the very mismatch NSVQ is criticized for.

Generation results are mixed rather than clearly superior: in Table 2/7, DiVeQ is often outperformed by STE/EMA at several codebook sizes, and the reported wins concentrate on small codebooks; the 'consistent improvement' framing overstates the evidence.

The speech results raise concerns about evaluation strength: PESQ values around 1.4–1.75 are unusually low even for a Bearer [REDACTED] (typical usable codecs achieve well above 2), suggesting the deliberately simplified DAC setup may not reflect a meaningful operating regime.

The misalignment analysis is informal: rate–distortion violations plus t-SNE plots are used to 'confirm' the misalignment hypothesis and to justify claims of SF-DiVeQ's immunity, without any rigorous diagnostic or quantitative criterion beyond eyeballing plots.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem (making vector quantization differentiable while preserving hard assignments) and offers a clean reparameterization-based solution that keeps the forward pass consistent with nearest-codeword assignment.

Extensive and convincing empirical evaluation across three different application domains (VQ-VAE image compression, VQGAN image generation, DAC speech coding), five image datasets, and multiple codebook sizes, with standard metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, FID, LSD, MFCC, PESQ, STOI).

Thorough ablation studies: batch size, learning rate, variance σ², codebook replacement, SF-DiVeQ initialization, and Residual VQ extension. The variance ablation supports the claim that σ² need not be tuned.
The qualitative and quantitative analysis of codebook–latent misalignment (t-SNE plots, rate-distortion argument) is an interesting and useful diagnostic contribution for the community.

Methods are presented as drop-in replacements with no auxiliary losses, and the paper provides comprehensive implementation details, a reproducibility statement, code, and generated/decompressed samples for subjective evaluation.
The variants (DiVeQ-detach, SF-DiVeQ-detach) and the improved codebook replacement strategy add practical value.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: DiVeQ is a relatively small modification of NSVQ (adding a directional bias to the noise vector so zq points at the nearest codeword), and SF-DiVeQ builds directly on SFVQ from the same group. The conceptual leap over prior work is incremental, even if the practical gains are real.

There is some tension with the paper's core claims: Table 1 advertises 'no complicated parameter tuning' and 'no auxiliary loss terms,' yet the method relies on a proposed codebook replacement heuristic with replacement schedules, discard thresholds, and, for SF-DiVeQ, a custom two-phase initialization (skipping quantization for two epochs and initializing the codebook from recent latents). These are effectively additional heuristics/hyperparameters, and the comparison fairness versus baselines deserves closer scrutiny (though the random-initialization ablation partly mitigates this).

The interpretation of results relies partly on an ad hoc 'misalignment' hypothesis (rate-distortion theory violations) rather than a direct causal analysis; the evidence is circumstantial (t-SNE visualizations and highlighted cases).

NSVQ performs strikingly poorly in the VQGAN experiments (FID > 60 everywhere), which is surprising given prior published results; the paper should better justify baseline configurations to rule out unfair or suboptimal treatment of competitors.

Train–test behavior of SF-DiVeQ differs from training (inference maps to the nearest point on the space-filling curve rather than argmin over codewords), so its claimed 'no train–test mismatch' advantage deserves a more careful analysis; similarly, the inference procedure's added cost is not quantified.

No analysis of computational overhead (e.g., noise sampling, distance computations for curve quantization) or training cost relative to STE/EMA baselines, which matters for a method proposed as a practical default.
Some misalignment cases still occur for DiVeQ itself (e.g., lr=10⁻³, 11-bit codebook), slightly weakening the claimed robustness advantage of the proposed family.

Codebook and latent dimensionality ranges tested are limited (mostly 8–13 bits, D=256/8); behavior at very large codebooks or with modern large-scale setups (e.g., full-size DAC, video codecs) is untested.
